title: Indian IT Stocks Surge 17% in July as Global Investors Flee the AI Trade
excerpt: The Nifty IT index posted its strongest month in six years as a global rotation out of AI-heavy markets turned India's lack of chip exposure into an unlikely advantage.
body:
• The Nifty IT index surged 16.8% in July, its strongest monthly performance in six years, as global investors rotated out of AI-heavy markets in South Korea and Taiwan.
  • Foreign investors bought $1.6 billion of Indian equities in July after selling $29 billion in the first half of the year.
  • HSBC, UBS, and Goldman Sachs all upgraded India in recent weeks, calling it the "obvious destination" for money leaving concentrated AI bets.
  • India's lack of direct AI chip exposure, long seen as a weakness, is now being reframed as portfolio diversification against a crowded tech trade.

Indian software exporters have staged a dramatic comeback. The Nifty IT index jumped 16.8% in July — its best month since 2020 — while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 21% and South Korea's benchmark dropped 24%.

The divergence is the widest since 1999, according to a Goldman Sachs note dated July 29. And it marks a sharp reversal for Indian equities, which lagged Asian peers for more than a year as global capital chased AI-linked plays in East Asia and the United States.

The Great Rotation

The trigger was a growing unease about the durability of AI capital spending. As doubts crept into semiconductor and hyperscaler valuations, portfolio managers began trimming positions in markets heavily weighted toward chips and AI infrastructure — chiefly South Korea and Taiwan.

India, with no major chipmaker or AI model builder in its benchmark indexes, became the default destination.

"India has emerged as the obvious destination for investors trimming their exposure to North Asian and U.S. technology stocks."

— Todd McClone, portfolio manager, William Blair Investment Management

McClone's firm, which oversees about $65 billion, started turning positive on India in April and added to positions in June after the Reserve Bank of India took steps to stabilize the rupee.

The rotation has been swift. Foreign investors, who dumped $29.3 billion of Indian equities in the first six months of 2026, bought $1.6 billion in July alone. That modest number understates the shift in sentiment: HSBC upgraded India to "neutral" from "underweight," UBS lifted its rating to "attractive," and both Goldman Sachs and Bernstein flagged the prospect of a second-half Nifty 50 rebound.

IT Stocks Lead the Pack

The biggest beneficiaries have been the software services giants. HCLTech surged 25.7% in July after beating quarterly estimates and approving fresh investment in an Indian AI data center. Infosys, TCS, and Tech Mahindra climbed between 12.9% and 17.6%.

The broader market followed, with the Nifty 50 rising 2% in July to post consecutive monthly gains for the first time this year. Eleven of 16 major sectors ended the month higher. Small-caps and mid-caps rose 2.5% and 1.8%, respectively.

Not Quite Anti-AI

The "anti-AI" label is somewhat misleading. India is not absent from the AI ecosystem — it is playing a different role in it.

Over 40% of Indian employees report using AI every day, double the global average, according to the ADP Research Institute. Google, Microsoft, and Amazon have collectively committed $57 billion to AI infrastructure in India over the next five years. Adani Group has pledged $100 billion and Blackstone $30 billion.

The more accurate frame, according to Manishi Raychaudhuri of Emmer Capital Partners, is "anti-AI-concentration" — a bet on a market where tech exposure is diversified rather than concentrated in a handful of chip stocks.

Risks on the Horizon

The rally is not without headwinds. Oil prices spiked over 30% in early July after the U.S.-Iran ceasefire collapsed, and the rupee remains down 6.5% against the dollar this year. Consumer inflation hit 4.4% in June, above the RBI's 4% target, with food prices adding upward pressure amid a weak monsoon.

"If crude prices settle down and Middle East tensions ease, India becomes a very attractive trade going forward, given domestic economic strength."

— Gaurav Didwania, fund manager, Qode

Whether the rotation proves durable depends on two factors: a sustained recovery in corporate earnings after several lackluster quarters, and a de-escalation in the Middle East that keeps energy costs in check.

What to Watch

Indian IT earnings for the September quarter will be the first real test of whether the rally has fundamental backing beyond rotation flows. Analysts are watching deal pipelines closely — if AI-driven demand starts showing up in order books at Infosys and TCS, the "anti-AI" narrative may need a complete rewrite.
